check_in.question: Should cancelled orders be ignored when finding a customer's first and second order? Returned orders would still count. Options: Ignore cancelled orders (returned still count); Count cancelled orders too; Ignore both cancelled and returned orders. I'd suggest: Ignore cancelled orders (returned still count), unless you prefer otherwise. (It changes who counts as a first-time customer, which year they fall in, and the repeat rate headline number.)
check_in.answer: Ignore cancelled orders and keep returned ones counted. That's the standard way to measure real purchases, so go with your suggestion.

check_in.question: For the recent groups that do not have 12 months of history yet (Oct 2025 onward), how should the rate be shown? Options: Rate so far only, labeled 'not final'; Also add a same-time comparison, such as the 6-month repeat rate for every year; Hide these groups until complete. I'd suggest: Rate so far only, labeled 'not final', unless you prefer otherwise. (Without a same-time comparison, 2025 Q4 and 2026 will look lower than earlier years just because they have had less time to reorder.)
check_in.answer: Go with the same-time comparison, such as the 6-month repeat rate for every year, along with the "not final" labels. I need to know whether 2026 really dropped, and without a like-for-like measure the recent groups will look worse just because they've had less time to reorder.

scores.comment: Strength: the brief matches the real need closely. It measures the 12-month repeat rate by year of first order, splits out the US from international countries, and asks how the rate changed rather than assuming a drop. It is also candid about limits: customers who ordered before 2019 will look new, there is no data on loyalty offers, and the data can't explain causes. Gap: the main 2026 comparison is not like-for-like. Partial rates are set against full 12-month rates, and the same-elapsed-time comparison is only offered as an option. Splitting 2025 into complete and incomplete parts also leaves the main view unclear, so a manager would likely ask for a fix before signing off.
